Overview — what was measured and how fast

We fitted a real optical spectrum of a galaxy with a physically motivated model of 21 numbers, several times over: with the existing CPU code path and with the new GPU code path, each using all the nested sampling machinery it has. The model and the data are identical in every run. The GPU finished in 6.3 min; 16 CPU cores needed 83.7 min (13.3× faster), and a single core needed 8.9 h (84.7× faster).

The short version

  • What we fit: one spectrum of the quasar IRAS 07546+3928 from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), a public survey. The spectrum covers 59,146 pixels (wavelength 4200–6900 Å).
  • The model: a smooth continuum + iron emission + 11 emission lines. The three hydrogen lines are each split into a narrow (slow gas) and a broad (fast gas) component; the forbidden lines get a narrow component, with a broad wing added for [O III] — 21 free numbers in total.
  • Two samplers: nested sampling explores the posterior — it maps out which parameter values are plausible. The existing code uses dynesty with astropy models on the CPU; the new code uses JNesty with jax models, which can run on the gpu.
  • Same stopping rule: both stop when the remaining uncertainty in the logz (evidence) is below 0.01 — the "dlogz" criterion. The answer is therefore not a premature one.
  • Result: the two paths find the same fit. Every one of the 21 numbers agrees to better than 0.1 of its own error bar; reduced χ² is identical. The evidence differs slightly between samplers, and so does it between two runs of the same sampler — see the results page for what that does and does not mean.

Timings, side by side

RunWall clockLikelihood calls log evidencereduced χ²
dynesty, one CPU core8.92 h2,758,067114271.0 ± 0.641.98
dynesty, 16 CPU cores83.7 min2,578,496114284.7 ± 0.611.98
JNesty on GPU6.3 min2,910,785114264.5 ± 0.641.98

"Likelihood calls" is how many times the model was compared with the data. Each sampler counts its own calls, and a call costs one model evaluation; the two columns are therefore indicative rather than identical, because the samplers decide differently how many proposals to try before accepting a point. The wall clock in the first column is what matters.

Why the speed-up is this large

A likelihood (how well a given parameter set matches the data) had to be evaluated 2.9 million times before the answer settled. So the speed-up is mostly about how long one evaluation takes:

What this does and does not show

  • It shows that the same scientific answer comes out, and that it comes out much faster on the GPU.
  • It does not show that the GPU makes every fit 20× faster. The gain grows with the size of the model: a small window around one line gains ~4–6×, because then the sampler's own bookkeeping, not the model, is the bottleneck.
  • The GPU is used as a single device; the CPU comparison also gives the "all 16 cores" number, so the comparison is fair in both directions.

Reproducing it

Everything on these pages comes from three commands (run from the repository root): 

python develop/dev_jax/run_sdss_fit.py --config jnesty-gpu       --nlive 400 --dlogz 0.01
python develop/dev_jax/run_sdss_fit.py --config dynesty-serial   --nlive 400 --dlogz 0.01
python develop/dev_jax/run_sdss_fit.py --config dynesty-parallel --processes 16 --nlive 400 --dlogz 0.01
python develop/dev_jax/make_report.py

The model itself lives in develop/dev_jax/sdss_agn.py; running that file on its own prints every prior and checks that the CPU and GPU models agree. The fit is not seeded from a previous solution: both samplers start from the priors alone.

The model — what the fit is made of, in plain words

A fit is only as good as the model. This page explains every ingredient in plain words, and why the model has 21 free numbers rather than 4 or 400.

1. What the data are

A spectrum is light split by wavelength: the horizontal axis is wavelength (here in Ångström, 1 Å = 0.1 nm) and the vertical axis is flux, how much light arrives per unit wavelength. We use the SDSS spectrum of IRAS 07546+3928, a galaxy whose centre hosts a supermassive black hole.

  • redshift: the galaxy moves away from us, which stretches every wavelength by a factor (1 + z). We divide it out, so the plot is in the rest-frame — wavelengths as they would be measured next to the galaxy.
  • dereddening: dust in our own Milky Way dims and reddens the light. We correct for it using the measured colour excess of this line of sight.
  • pixel: the spectrum is sampled every 0.046 Å. That is much finer than the instrument can actually resolve (see lsf below), which is normal for SDSS and is why the model has to include the instrument.

2. The pieces of the model

PieceIn plain wordsPhysics
Power-law continuum The smooth underlying glow, brighter at one end of the spectrum than the other. Light from the accretion disc around the black hole.
Fe II template A forest of thousands of blended iron lines that looks like a bumpy pseudo-continuum, strongest bluewards of Hβ. Iron gas in the same fast-moving clouds that produce the broad lines.
Hα, Hβ, Hγ The three brightest hydrogen lines, each modelled as narrow + broad gaussians. Hydrogen recombining: narrow-line gas far from the black hole, broad-line gas close to it.
[O III] 4959, 5007 The strongest forbidden lines, with a narrow core and a broad wing. Doubly ionised oxygen in the narrow-line region, sometimes with an outflow.
[N II] 6548, 6583 Sits right next to Hα and is easy to confuse with it. Ionised nitrogen; its two lines have a fixed 1:3 brightness ratio.
[S II] 6716, 6731 A pair of faint lines that is sensitive to how dense the gas is. Ionised sulphur; the ratio of the pair measures gas density.
[O I] 6300, 6364A faint pair from neutral oxygen. Neutral gas, often with a broad component in outflows.
He II 4686, [O III] 4363Two faint single lines. Singly ionised helium and the temperature-sensitive oxygen line.

3. How one line is described

A gaussian is the bell curve: three numbers (peak height, centre, width) describe it completely. Real line profiles are close enough to a sum of a few bell curves that this is standard practice. Each Balmer line therefore gets:

  • a narrow Gaussian (narrow-line) — gas moving at a few hundred km/s;
  • a broad Gaussian (broad-line) — gas moving at thousands of km/s, swirling around the black hole;
  • a fixed wavelength — the line's laboratory value — plus a velocity shift.

Widths are quoted in km/s rather than Å: that converts a wavelength width into the speed of the gas that produced it, which is the physically interesting quantity. The relation between the Gaussian width (σ) and the full width at half maximum (fwhm) is FWHM = 2.355 σ.

4. Why 21 numbers, not 60

Eleven components, each with 3–9 parameters, would be 60+ free numbers. We use two tricks, both standard in the field, to keep it at 21:

  • Ties. Some numbers are physically the same for several lines: all narrow lines share one velocity shift and one width; all broad Balmer lines share one shift and one width. A tie is simply a rule saying "this parameter equals that one", so the sampler only varies it once.
  • Atomic physics. The two lines of a doublet ([O III], [N II], [S II], [O I]) have fixed brightness ratios, fixed by quantum mechanics. We impose them, so a doublet costs one amplitude instead of two.

5. The instrument is part of the model

No spectrograph measures a line exactly: it smears it with its line-spread function (LSF). SDSS has a resolving-power R ≈ 2000, meaning it can separate two wavelengths that differ by only 1 part in 2000 — at 5000 Å that is 2.5 Å. If we ignore this smearing, the model is forced to reproduce the instrument's profile with the gas's velocity width, which gives nonsense (the fit runs to the prior edges). We therefore convolve the whole model with a Gaussian of that width before comparing to the data.

6. The priors: what we allow before looking at the data

A prior is the range a parameter is allowed to take. Ours are deliberately wide, and they are derived from the data's own flux range rather than from a preliminary fit — so nothing is hidden in a hand-tuned starting point:

  • every emission-line peak may be anywhere from 10-3 to twice the brightest pixel of the spectrum, with a log-uniform prior (equal probability per factor of ten, which is the right choice for a quantity spanning orders of magnitude);
  • narrow-line widths: 30–1000 km/s (FWHM 70–2400 km/s);
  • broad Balmer widths: 500–20000 km/s;
  • the continuum slope may be anything from steeply falling to steeply rising.

7. The same model, twice

The CPU model is an astropy Fittable1DModel. The GPU model is a jax class written to evaluate the identical arithmetic. Both are built by one function in develop/dev_jax/sdss_agn.py, from a shared list of components, so they cannot drift apart. Two tests show it: at the best-fit parameters the two models agree to 1.5×10-15 of the peak flux, i.e. to float64 rounding error; and at 25 random points drawn from the prior the two likelihood values agree to 3×10-5 out of ~105 — a relative difference of 3×10-10. The GPU path is not approximating anything.

Results — the numbers, the fit quality, the agreement

The fit, the numbers behind it, and how much the answer depends on which sampler ran.

1. The fit itself

Reduced χ² per degree of freedom is 1.98, and the scatter of the residuals is 1.40 error bars. A perfect fit would give 1.00; real spectra with a simplified model usually land between 1 and 3, so this is a healthy fit.

6. Priors versus posteriors

7. Do the two code paths agree?

Runlog evidenceError Offset from meanreduced χ²
dynesty, one CPU core114271.0±0.64-2.361.978
dynesty, 16 CPU cores114284.7±0.61+11.291.978
JNesty on GPU114264.5±0.64-8.931.978

The parameters agree to a fraction of their error bars. Across all 21 fitted quantities the two samplers differ by at most 0.05 of a standard error (median 0.01), and the largest relative difference of any quoted value is 0.17% — that one is a velocity of 0.08 km/s. This is what "the GPU version gives the same answer" means in practice: the numbers you would put in a paper are identical.

The log evidence is a different matter, and it is worth being precise about. It is a single number saying how well the model explains the data overall (bigger is better), and here the two samplers differ by 20.2 nats while each claims an error of about 0.6. Two things follow. First, the GPU implementation is not the noisy one: making JNesty work twice as hard (nlive 400 → 800) moved its answer by 0.3 nats, so it has converged. Second, and this is the decisive check, the same sampler run twice on different numbers of CPU cores — one core versus sixteen, identical code, identical settings — gives 13.6 nats of its own, 22 times its quoted error. So the gap between codes is ordinary integrator scatter, not GPU arithmetic. The error bars nested samplers report for log Z describe the scatter of one code's paths, not the difference between two integration schemes. Use the evidence ratios with that in mind; for parameter estimates, which is what almost everyone wants, the runs are interchangeable.

Caveats, stated plainly

  • The line profiles are simplified. Real broad lines have longer wings than a Gaussian. At the very top of [O III] and Hβ the model is off by a few σ over a handful of pixels. This is a property of the 2-component line model, and it is the same for both code paths.
  • 3% systematic error. Besides the 1% photon noise measured from the spectrum, we add 3% in quadrature to stand for flux-calibration error, the iron-template shape and the imperfections of a single power law. Without it, χ²/dof would be ~6 — a statement about the model's simplicity, not about the samplers.
  • Na D. The galaxy's stellar sodium absorption at 5885 Å is not in the model; those pixels get 3× larger errors instead of being cut, so that the wavelength grid stays uniform (the lsf kernel needs that).
  • Absolute scale. Widths and ratios are meaningful; absolute fluxes are in the file's arbitrary units.

Glossary — every technical term, explained

Every technical word used on these pages, in the order you are likely to meet it. Terms are explained for a reader who knows what a spectrum is but not what a "live point" or "dlogz" means.

Spectrum
Light split up by wavelength. The horizontal axis is wavelength, the vertical axis is how much light arrives at each wavelength. A spectrum tells you which atoms and which physical conditions produced the light.
Wavelength
The distance between two crests of a light wave, measured in Ångström (1 Å = 10-10 m). Visible light spans roughly 4000–7000 Å.
Flux
The amount of light energy arriving per unit area per unit time per unit wavelength. In these pages it is in the FITS file's own arbitrary units, so only relative values matter.
Pixel
One wavelength bin of the spectrum. This spectrum has one pixel every 0.046 Å.
Redshift (z)
Because the universe expands, light from a distant galaxy arrives stretched to longer wavelengths by a factor (1 + z). For IRAS 07546+3928, z = 0.0953, so every wavelength is 9.5% longer than in the galaxy's own frame.
Rest frame
Wavelengths as they would be measured by an observer sitting next to the galaxy, i.e. after dividing out the redshift. All plots here are in the rest frame, so the lines appear at their laboratory wavelengths.
Dereddening
Correcting for dust absorption by our own Milky Way, which both dims and reddens extragalactic light. We apply the standard Cardelli, Clayton & Mathis (1989) law with E(B−V) = 0.176.
Continuum
The smooth part of the spectrum, without the sharp lines. Here it is modelled as a power law: brightness proportional to wavelength−α.
Emission line
A sharp spike of extra light at one specific wavelength, produced when an electron drops to a lower energy level in an atom. Each element has its own set of wavelengths, which is how we know what the gas is made of.
Forbidden line
An emission line from a transition that is so slow that, in a laboratory, the atom is disturbed before it can emit. In the extremely thin gas of space it happens anyway. Written with square brackets, like [O III].
Narrow line
Light from gas moving slowly (a few hundred km/s), far from the black hole — the narrow-line region, hundreds to thousands of light years across.
Broad line
Light from gas whirling rapidly (thousands of km/s) around the black hole, within a few light years. Fast motion smears the line out in wavelength (the Doppler effect).
Gaussian
The bell curve, described by a peak height, a centre and a width σ. A line profile is modelled as a sum of a few Gaussians.
σ (sigma)
Two meanings, both standard. (1) The width of a Gaussian, in km/s. (2) The measurement error of a data point; residuals are quoted 'in σ', so +2 means 'two error bars above the model'.
FWHM
Full Width at Half Maximum: the width of a line measured at half its peak height. For a Gaussian, FWHM = 2.355 σ. Astronomers quote it because it can be read off a plot directly.
Line-spread function (LSF)
The profile a spectrograph imposes on an infinitely sharp line: a real instrument smears every line into a small bell curve. Ignoring it makes a fit try to explain instrumental smearing with the gas's own motion.
Resolving power (R)
R = wavelength / smallest resolvable wavelength difference. SDSS has R ≈ 2000, so at 5000 Å it can just separate features 2.5 Å apart.
Convolution
The mathematical operation of smearing one function with another: take the model, spread every point of it into the instrument's profile, and add up. Written f ∗ g.
Fe II (iron) emission
Thousands of blended emission lines from singly ionised iron. Together they look like a bumpy extra continuum, strongest bluewards of Hβ, and are modelled with a template spectrum scaled and blurred by the fit.
Tie (tied parameter)
A rule that forces one parameter to equal a function of others, e.g. 'all narrow lines share the width of [O III]'. Ties encode physics and remove parameters the data cannot constrain independently.
Prior
What you allow a parameter to be before looking at the data: a range (and a shape, e.g. uniform or log-uniform). Wide priors mean the answer comes from the data.
Posterior
The probability distribution of the parameters after the data are taken into account. It answers 'given this spectrum, which parameter values are plausible, and how precisely?'.
Likelihood
How probable the observed data are for a given set of parameters. For Gaussian errors it is exp(−χ²/2), so maximising the likelihood means minimising χ².
χ² (chi-squared)
The sum over all pixels of ((data − model) / error)². It is the natural measure of misfit when errors are Gaussian: 1 per pixel means a typical deviation of one error bar.
Degrees of freedom
The number of data points minus the number of fitted parameters. Dividing χ² by it gives the 'reduced χ²', which is ~1 for a good fit regardless of how many pixels there are.
Nested sampling
A way of mapping the posterior and computing the evidence at the same time: keep a set of 'live points' spread over the prior, repeatedly discard the worst one and replace it with a better one, so the live set shrinks onto the high-likelihood region. It handles awkward, multi-peaked posteriors that gradient methods miss.
Live points (nlive)
The number of parameter sets carried simultaneously by nested sampling. More live points means a more reliable map of the posterior, at proportionally higher cost.
log Z (log evidence)
The integral of likelihood × prior over all parameters, i.e. the average likelihood the model achieves over the whole prior. It is the number to compare models with, and the by-product of nested sampling.
dlogz (stopping threshold)
The estimated amount of evidence still unaccounted for when the sampler stops. Requiring dlogz < 0.01 means 'less than 1% of the evidence may still be missing', which forces the sampler to run until the answer is stable.
Sampler
The algorithm that explores the posterior. Here: dynesty (CPU, the existing code) and JNesty (GPU-capable, the new code).
jit (just-in-time compilation)
Turning a Python function into machine code the first time it is called. The compile cost is paid once; every later call is fast. That is why compiled timings here exclude the first call.
vmap (vectorised map)
Telling JAX to run a function on many inputs at once, laid out as an array. On a GPU this fills the device with work instead of evaluating points one by one.
JAX
A numerical library that compiles array code (like NumPy) for CPUs or GPUs. The GPU model in GalSpec is written in JAX so the same code runs on either device.
float64 / float32
How many bits a computer uses for a real number. float64 (~16 digits) is the default here, because likelihood values differ in the 10th digit; float32 is twice as fast on some GPUs but only accurate to ~7 digits, which we offer as an option (GALSPEC_JAX_X64=0) rather than the default.
GPU (graphics processing unit)
A chip with thousands of simple cores. Bad at sequential logic, excellent at doing the same arithmetic to a million numbers at once — which is what evaluating a model on a 59 146-pixel spectrum is.
Corner plot
A grid of histograms: the diagonal shows each parameter's posterior, the off-diagonal panels show pairs, revealing correlations. A compact way to see a 23-dimensional result.
Credible interval
The range containing a given probability (here 68%, i.e. 1σ) under the posterior. The Bayesian counterpart of a confidence interval.
